text: Meridian Outfitters, a small online retailer, needs a first real AWS environment for a new order-lookup tool: a web tier the public can reach, an app tier that only the web tier is allowed to reach, and shared storage both tiers can read and write. This lesson builds all three, using the same aws CLI from Chapter 5, in the order a SysOps admin would actually run it against a live account.

Everything lives inside one VPC, carved into two subnets the way Chapter 4's CIDR planning describes. 10.50.1.0/24 becomes meridian-public-subnet, destined for the web tier. 10.50.2.0/24 becomes meridian-private-subnet, destined for the app tier. Neither one is actually public or private yet on its own — that status is entirely decided by what gets attached to each subnet in the steps that follow.

A subnet only becomes public through three things acting together: a route table entry pointing 0.0.0.0/0 at an attached internet gateway, and map-public-ip-on-launch switched on so new instances actually receive a public address. Skip either half and the subnet looks correctly configured but behaves privately anyway — exactly the kind of gap Lesson 31's troubleshooting case study walks through in detail.

Two security groups get created, one per tier, and both start with zero inbound rules — locked down by default. meridian-web1 launches into the public subnet with associate-public-ip-address set, so it gets a public IP immediately. meridian-app1 launches into the private subnet with that flag omitted, so it gets none. Same AMI, same t3.micro instance type, two completely different reachability stories.

Neither tier's local disk is the right home for order data both instances need to read and write. Chapter 3's answer is S3: a bucket named meridian-outfitters-app-data, created with a single aws s3api create-bucket call. The company name in the bucket name isn't a style choice — S3's bucket namespace is global across every AWS account, so a generic name like app-data is almost certainly already taken.

The environment is standing end to end — VPC, subnets, two EC2 instances, one S3 bucket — but every security group is still empty and nothing is being watched or alerted on yet. Lesson 30 picks up exactly there: scoping each security group to the traffic it actually needs, swapping in an IAM role instead of any hardcoded access key, and adding the monitoring and cost guardrails to match.
